keyFindings.description: The justification for never using /healthz as a liveness probe may be wrong on a modern kubelet, which is said to stop liveness and startup probes when a pod begins terminating (SyncTerminatingPod calling StopLivenessAndStartup before killPod), so a liveness probe would not kill the container mid-drain for an ordinary pod deletion; the case it would cover is a process signalled while its pod keeps running. [INFERENCE] I could not settle this against the cluster's own Kubernetes version from here: the behaviour was reported as the opposite in kubernetes/kubernetes#107473, closed not-planned about four years ago, so it has plainly changed at some point and which side the deployment is on depends on its version. The recommendation itself is unaffected either way — readiness, not liveness — and over-caution here costs nothing. The same sentence stands in AGENTS.md:3027-3029 and routes_table.go:173-175.

The fan-out's guarantee is still stated as 'within seconds, except while a pod's listener is redialing' in operate.md:422-425, AGENTS.md:2476-2479, reread/reread.go:142-149, concepts.md:235-244, guides/revoke-a-session.md:99-103 and guides/troubleshooting.md:92, while manage-a-secret.md now states the complete set. A connected peer also falls outside when its Refresh fails (reread.go:175-178 logs and does not retry) and when that Refresh succeeds on stale metadata (policy/current.go:144-150 accepts an unchanged result with a nil error; secrets/gcp.go reads GetSecret, which Google documents as eventually consistent). The revoke guide is the one of these that is operational advice rather than an architecture sketch.

'pgxpool's own background work would end with that context' is false for the pinned pgx. NewWithConfig passes ctx only to createIdleResources, and backgroundHealthCheck's loop returns on p.closeChan and nothing else (pgx v5.11.0 pgxpool/pool.go:334-337,506-517, read in the module cache). Both minimums are zero here anyway. Keeping context.Background() is right; the reason given for it is not, and a reader could infer that cancelling the construction context is cleanup when only Close is.

'the fan-out deliberately drops r's cancellation, which fires as soon as the answer is written' gives the wrong event and the wrong order. A request's context is cancelled when the client connection closes or when ServeHTTP returns, not when the answer is written, and the notify at :129 runs before writeJSON at :135, so the cancellation this detaches from has not fired at that point. The detachment is right; what it protects against is a caller that hangs up mid-reread and the request's own 45-second deadline, which is what the comment should say.

Two counts in the redial row are one short. It says 'the three rows below' and 'of the four': the rows below it are :366 (binding before the reread listener has had an answer), :367 (serving without the boot's catch-up policy load), :368 (the other pods were not told to reread a secret) and :369 (a notification's reread of a secret did not run) — four below, five in all, which is the number manage-a-secret.md's own table gives.

The class, rather than an instance. Five consecutive rounds of reading prose against the code beside it have each found more, and this round's six are of one kind: of them only the Kubernetes probe sentence describes behaviour anyone can execute, and the other five explain why code is shaped as it is. That is the surface the decomposition on the Fast-follow line reduces — main.go at about 650 lines with its boot and stop sequence inline, limits.go at 316 mostly comment — and it is the remedy that scales where a sixth sweep does not. Recorded as the reviewer's reason for carrying these six as a Fast-follow rather than a round.

roundFourFindingsVerified: Finding 1, the retag clearance: the retag-again remedy no longer offers one. The section now leads with 'The way to avoid the question is not to convert' — create the secret with its kind under a name no agent holds a grant on — and the conversion path says in its own bullet that a second exit 0 says only that the answering process has the new tags, that it says nothing about the peers and no log line will, and why: a peer's reread reads the one name too and can succeed on stale Secret Manager metadata, the WARN fires only on an error, and the notification is asynchronous besides. That is the shape the architect ruled for, weaker and true rather than stronger and wrong.
Finding 2: concepts.md:235 is scoped to POST /v1/secrets/{name}/reread and states the miss path as deliberately local.

Finding 3: operate.md:365 no longer promises /healthz 200 through a redial; it says losing the LISTEN does not by itself fail readiness and that the two often appear together, a 200 beside the line being the case to worry about.

Finding 4: reread.go:156 now says 'a Refresh that fails' and states what happens to a refused name instead — RefreshOne answers it with a Lookup and a nil error that the supplied Refresh discards, so the policy's own refusal line records it and nothing in that package fires.

Finding 5, the three stop-path statements, all corrected and the correction checked rather than read: the comment now says st.Close never touches the hijacked connection and that pglisten's own deferred close ends it, which the code gives (store.go conn.Hijack, pglisten/listener.go:146,218-221); the loops now run until Shutdown returns 'having answered the last request, or having spent its 60-second allowance'; and writeTimeout is now 'the longest exchange the server itself allows a request past its headers', with the new sentence about a connection that never sends one verified against the standard library — net/http's closeIdleConns treats a StateNew connection with no headers for five seconds as idle (Go issue 22682, server.go:3303-3315).

thermonuclear.deepReview: APPROVE — no finding. It checked the new-name recommendation against the code rather than accepting it: the CLI builds the kind and rollback-guard tags before creating the secret, AWS sends tags and value in one CreateSecret, GCP creates the secret with its annotations before the first value, and the loader encodes the kind into the source that evaluation freezes into the request, so a name never served as ordinary has no grant that can release a raw value and creating-then-granting opens no second window. No defect in the reread route's buckets, the drain, the watchdog, the catch-up, the NOTIFY path, the hijacked connection, store.Close, the developer workflow or the CI job's pins.
thermonuclear.codeQuality: CHANGES — the comment-against-code sweep is not clean: the Kubernetes probe justification, the fan-out guarantee still stated as redial-only in six places, the pgxpool lifetime claim, the detached-notify cancellation event, and the redial row's counts. All six are carried as the one Fast-follow rather than as a round; none changes behaviour, hides an error or breaks a gate, and the reviewer's reason is recorded in the findings.
